title: Jones Beach Drift Whale Rights
summary: Tackapousha and Native communities asserted rights to valuable marine resources, including drift whales along the south shore barrier beaches. The modern Jones Beach landscape is therefore also a place to discuss Native jurisdiction, marine economies, and colonial legal change.
address_label: Jones Beach barrier beach landscape, Jones Inlet vicinity
ancestral_territory_note: Linked to Merrick Ancestral Land as part of the south shore/barrier beach history; also connected with Massapequa leadership and overlapping regional authority.
why_this_matters: Jones Beach is usually remembered as a modern public beach, but older records connect the barrier island to Native marine rights and coastal economies. The site carries histories of Indigenous jurisdiction and resource knowledge within a familiar public landscape.
introduction_content: Drift whales provided valuable resources along Long Island’s barrier beaches. Tackapousha and other Native leaders defended rights to these whales as part of their authority over coastal lands and waters.1
history_content:
In a July 26, 2023 report for The Long Island Advocate, Cody Hmelar described meeting Indigenous canoeists and supporters at Jones Beach during a journey drawing attention to Native sovereignty and the Montaukett Indian Nation. His podcast records Chenae Bullock, who led the Boston-to-New York City portion, and Montaukett historian Sandi Brewster-Walker discussing continuing Native presence.2

The journey brought Indigenous sovereignty and continuing Native presence into a familiar public beach landscape.2

A coast of rights and relationships

A whale washed ashore could provide food and other valuable materials. Control of the carcass was therefore also a question of authority over the coast. John A. Strong places Tackapousha within the history of Native leaders negotiating with colonists over drift whales and other resources. These negotiations belong alongside disputes about meadows and planting land: rights to a homeland included what its waters and beaches provided.1

The 2023 canoe journey brought a contemporary expression of Indigenous sovereignty to these waters. Reporting from Jones Beach records Chenae Bullock and Montaukett historian Sandi Brewster-Walker speaking about Native presence and recognition. The journey connects the coast’s history with Native people traveling, teaching, and asserting relationships with their homelands today.2
